argument: Specialized processors operate largely locally, while a subset of information gains conscious access when recurrent amplification makes it globally available to attention, memory, report, and control systems. The theory predicts late, widespread, and task-dependent ignition signatures.
boundary: Neural signatures vary with report requirements, attention, and task design.
Global availability is difficult to separate experimentally from consciousness itself.
claim: Specialized processors operate largely locally, while a subset of information gains conscious access when recurrent amplification makes it globally available to attention, memory, report, and control systems. The theory predicts late, widespread, and task-dependent ignition signatures.
interpretation: Keep this as a contested hypothesis. A broadcast-like software architecture is not evidence of phenomenal consciousness.
